title: TLS 1.3, certificates and mTLS
goal: By the end, you can explain what TLS hides on the way and what it leaves for anyone to see, how a certificate proves who a server is, what each message of the TLS 1.3 handshake does, and how to tell certificate failures apart by their error messages.
opening:
Picture yourself in a café, on its free Wi-Fi, paying a bill on your bank's website. Your laptop doesn't talk to the bank directly. Every packet goes first to the small Wi-Fi box behind the counter, then through a dozen other computers on the way. Any of them could read what passes. But the browser shows a padlock, so you relax.

The padlock is easy to over-trust. It feels like a sealed envelope, so it's natural to think nobody on the way learns anything. In fact the Wi-Fi box still sees which site you're visiting. And a lock on its own proves nothing about who holds the other key.

The lesson before this one, DNS: how a name becomes an address, showed how a program finds a server's address, and that a forged reply can send it somewhere else. In this lesson, we'll lock a connection with TLS, prove who is on the other end with a certificate, and break that proof three ways on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: In the café, your laptop sends a payment to `https://api.bank.example/authorize` over TLS 1.3, the newest version of the protocol behind the padlock. The café's Wi-Fi box records every packet. What can its owner read?
options: Nothing at all: the padlock means everything is hidden
The two computers' addresses, the site's name, and the size and timing of each chunk of data, but not what was sent
Everything, because the keys have to travel over the Wi-Fi too
The full web address, `/authorize` included, but not the card number
warmup.why: The very first message of the connection, the ClientHello, travels unlocked, and it names the server (in a field called SNI) so the server knows which certificate to show. The addresses, and the size and timing of every chunk, are visible too. What was sent is locked: the path `/authorize`, the card number and the answer. The keys never cross the Wi-Fi, which is where the third option goes wrong. Each side works them out from its own secret and the other side's public value, as the first section shows. A newer feature, Encrypted Client Hello, can hide the name too, where both sides support it.

sections.h: What the café's Wi-Fi box can read, and change
sections.body:
Let's look at what the Wi-Fi box sees. Computers talk by sending packets: small chunks of data, each with the sender's and receiver's addresses on the front. On its way, a packet crosses several routers, computers that pass each packet one step closer to where it's going. Each router reads the addresses to choose the next step. Nothing stops it from reading the rest.

Our running example is the coffee-shop payments app. When you tap your card, the app sends the card number and the amount to the bank that issued the card, and asks whether to approve the payment. In the lab, a pretend computer called client plays the app, server plays the bank, and router plays the Wi-Fi box between them. The Try it below sends a plain HTTP request from client to server and prints what router saw: the whole request, card number included. (HTTP is the set of rules web browsers and servers use to ask and answer.)

A router that can read can also write. It could change `amount=100.00` to `amount=900.00` before it passes the packet on. Each packet carries a checksum, a small number worked out from its bytes so the receiver can spot accidental damage. Anyone can work it out again, so the router fixes the checksum and neither end notices. Or the router could answer in the bank's place.

So a safe connection needs three things. Confidentiality: nobody on the path can read the bytes. Integrity: nobody can change them without being caught. Authentication: you know you're talking to the bank, not to whoever answered.

Start with the first two. Suppose both ends shared a secret number, a key. They could use a cipher, a method that scrambles data so that only someone with the key can unscramble it. The usual one is AES-GCM, a symmetric cipher: the same key locks and unlocks. It adds a 16-byte tag worked out from the key and the data, so changing one bit on the way breaks the tag. One core of a modern processor runs it at gigabytes per second, so this part is cheap. TLS (Transport Layer Security), the protocol behind the padlock, uses it for all your data. (A protocol is a set of rules that two programs follow to talk, and HTTP sent inside TLS is called HTTPS.)

The hard part is getting the key to both ends. You can't send it, because the router would read it. The answer is a **key exchange**, and it fits in a few small numbers. Both sides use two public numbers, 5 and 23. The client picks a secret, 6, and sends `5^6 mod 23 = 8`. (`^` means "to the power of", and `mod 23` means "the remainder after dividing by 23".) The server picks its own secret, 15, and sends `5^15 mod 23 = 19`. The client works out `19^6 mod 23 = 2`, and the server works out `8^15 mod 23 = 2`. Both now hold the same secret, 2. The router saw 5, 23, 8 and 19, and never the 2.

With numbers this small, you could find the 6 by trying every candidate. Real TLS uses X25519, the same idea done on a mathematical curve, with 32-byte public values. There, trying every candidate is out of reach for any computer built today.

That still isn't enough. Whoever controls the router can run one key exchange with you and a second one with the bank, and pass messages between the two. You'd have a well-locked connection to the attacker, which is a very private way to be robbed. The client needs proof of who sent the server's half of the exchange. Next, we'll build that proof: a certificate.

try.title: Read a payment on the router
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the lab network if it isn't running: `docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d`. It's a small pretend network made of containers, programs that each behave like a separate small computer. client sits on one network, called lan, and server on another, called wan. router joins the two, like the café's Wi-Fi box.

The first line below tells server to send its replies for lan through router, as you did in lesson 4 of this track. The second starts tcpdump on router in the background. tcpdump is a program that prints the packets passing through a computer, and `-A` prints the data of each packet to port 8080 as text. (A port is a number that picks out one program on a computer, here the web server.)

client then sends a made-up card payment to the small web server running on server. That web server, Python's `http.server`, answers 501 ("not implemented") because it doesn't accept a POST, the kind of request that sends data. That doesn't matter here. Predict before you run it: will router see the card number, and how many times?

code.title: in labs/
code.src:
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec server ip route replace 10.10.1.0/24 via 10.10.2.2
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec -d router sh -c 'tcpdump -i any -nn -A -l "tcp port 8080 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-push != 0" > /tmp/seen.txt 2>/dev/null'
sleep 1
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client curl -s -o /dev/null -d 'card=4242424242424242&amount=100.00' http://10.10.2.20:8080/authorize
sleep 1
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router sh -c 'pkill tcpdump; grep -a -o -E "(.*IP 10.10.1.10.*|POST /authorize HTTP/1.1|card=[0-9]+&amount=[0-9.]+)" /tmp/seen.txt'

From one run (TCP options trimmed):

```text

POST /authorize HTTP/1.1

Both copies hold the card number and the amount as plain text, in 192 bytes of HTTP. Your interface names and numbers may differ. The TLS Try its below capture the same kind of request and find only the server's name.

sections.h: Proving who answered: a certificate, and a chain back to someone you trust
sections.body:
The client must be sure that the server's half of the key exchange came from the bank. In the lab, the bank's server is called `api.pay.test`, a made-up name. The simplest plan is that every client keeps a list of every server's key. That breaks at once: there are millions of servers, and each one changes its key now and then.

One more tool first. A key pair is two numbers made together: a private key, which the owner keeps secret, and a public key, which anyone may have. Data signed with the private key can be checked with the public key. Only the owner can make the signature, and anyone can check it. That's a digital signature.

Now think of a passport. It ties a name to a photo, and a government you trust issued it. At the border, the officer checks the government's marks, checks the dates, and checks that your face matches the photo. A **certificate** does the same for a server. A certificate authority (CA), a company whose job is checking who owns a name, makes sure that whoever asks really controls `api.pay.test`. Then it signs a short document: this public key belongs to this name, from this date to that date. Its format is called X.509, and RFC 5280 describes it. (An RFC is one of the public documents that define how the internet's protocols work.) Here is the one the Try it makes:

```text
subject=CN = api.pay.test
issuer=O = Pay Test, CN = Pay Test Issuing CA 1
notBefore=Nov  7 21:19:33 2026 GMT
notAfter=Dec 22 21:19:33 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:api.pay.test
```

In the passport picture, the name is the server's name, the photo is the public key, and the government is the CA. The face check happens during the connection: the server signs the conversation with its private key, and the client checks it with the public key in the certificate. That's also where the picture breaks. A certificate is public, so a copy proves nothing. Only the private key can make the signature, and it never leaves the server.

Why trust the CA? Every client comes with a list of CA certificates it trusts without proof, its **trust store**. The JDK 25 in this track's labs (the Java Development Kit, the programs that compile and run Java) trusts 118 of them, called root CAs. A stolen root key would let the thief sign for any name, so roots are kept offline, away from any network. A root signs a few intermediate CAs, and an intermediate signs the certificates that servers use, called leaf certificates. A server sends its leaf and its intermediate. The client walks up this chain until it reaches a root it already has.

At each step the client checks four things. The signature checks out with the issuer's public key. The issuer is marked as a CA (`CA:TRUE`). Today is between the two dates. And for the leaf, the server's name is in the Subject Alternative Name (SAN), the certificate's list of names. The older CN (common name) field is ignored.

The most common failure is a server that doesn't send its intermediate. Browsers often fetch the missing one from an address written in the certificate. The JDK doesn't, so the site works in Chrome and fails in your Java program.

Certificates are getting shorter lives, so that a stolen key stays useful for less time. Let's Encrypt, a free CA that millions of websites use, issues 90-day certificates today. Its default moves to 64 days in February 2027 and to 45 days in February 2028. Nobody renews a certificate every 45 days by hand. **A certificate nobody renews stops working on a date you could have read. Automate the renewal.**

Next, we'll see where the certificate travels in the handshake, and when the keys get made.

try.title: Make a tiny CA and check a chain
steps: Start the lab box from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`. It's a Linux shell inside a container, with the network tools this track uses already installed.

`env/net/pki.sh` makes a root CA, an intermediate, a server certificate for `api.pay.test` and a client certificate for the last section. It uses nothing but openssl, a command-line tool for keys and certificates. Read the script afterwards: a CA is a key pair and a certificate, nothing more.
Check the server certificate twice, once with the intermediate and once without. Predict which check fails, and with what.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
bash /labs/env/net/pki.sh /tmp/pki
cd /tmp/pki
openssl x509 -in api.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted inter.pem api.pem
openssl verify -CAfile root.pem api.pem

try.expect:
From one run (the list of ten files cut to its first and last):

```text
api-chain.pem
...
root.pem
subject=CN = api.pay.test
issuer=O = Pay Test, CN = Pay Test Issuing CA 1
notBefore=Nov  7 21:19:33 2026 GMT
notAfter=Dec 22 21:19:33 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:api.pay.test
api.pem: OK
CN = api.pay.test
error 20 at 0 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
error api.pem: verification failed
```

The certificate is valid for 45 days from the moment you ran the script, and the name the client checks is in the Subject Alternative Name. With the intermediate on offer, the chain reaches the root and checks out. (`-untrusted` means "you may use these to build the chain, but don't trust them on their own".) Without it, openssl can't find who signed `api.pem`. That's error 20, the same failure a client hits when a server forgets to send its intermediate. Your dates will differ.

sections.h: The TLS 1.3 handshake: one round trip, then everything is locked
sections.body:
Put the pieces together and you have the handshake: the opening messages two programs swap before any real data. TLS 1.3, the current version, is written down in RFC 9846 (July 2026). It replaced RFC 8446, which most tools still cite, without changing the protocol.

The handshake needs one round trip, one message there and one answer back. It manages that with a guess. The client doesn't first ask which key exchange the server prefers. It guesses, and sends its public value in its very first message. TLS calls each kind of key exchange a group. Here are the messages, in order:

1. **ClientHello**, readable by anyone. It holds a random number and the cipher suites the client accepts (named sets of methods, such as `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`). It lists the versions it speaks (`supported_versions`, where TLS 1.3 is 0x0304, a number written in hexadecimal). It names the server it wants (SNI, server name indication), because one address can serve many names, each with its own certificate. It lists the application protocols the client speaks (ALPN, for example `h2` for HTTP/2, a newer version of HTTP, and `http/1.1`). And it carries key shares: public values for the groups the client guesses the server will pick.
2. **ServerHello**, also readable. The server picks a version, a cipher suite and one of the offered groups, and sends its own key share. Both sides can now work out the shared secret and the first keys. The router can't.
3. Locked from here on: **EncryptedExtensions** with the chosen application protocol, **Certificate** with the chain, and **CertificateVerify**, a signature over every handshake byte so far, made with the leaf's private key. Last comes **Finished**, which holds a MAC (message authentication code), a short code worked out from the bytes and a secret key. It proves that nobody changed a message on the way.
4. The client checks the chain and the name, checks the signature with the public key in the leaf, and sends its own Finished. Its first request goes in the same flight, the same batch of packets.

From then on, TLS sends data in records, locked chunks of up to 16 KB each.

Let's count the cost of a new connection to a bank 70 ms (thousandths of a second) away, there and back. First comes the handshake of TCP, the protocol underneath that delivers bytes in order and resends lost ones: one round trip (lesson 7 of this track, TCP connections). Then one round trip for TLS. That's 140 ms before the client may send, and the request needs another 35 ms to arrive: 175 ms before the bank sees your first byte. TLS 1.2, the version before, needed two round trips here, so TLS 1.3 saves one. A connection pool, a set of open connections that a program keeps and reuses, saves both.

If the guess is wrong, the server answers with a HelloRetryRequest naming a group it accepts, and the client pays one more round trip for a second ClientHello. That's why clients always include a share for x25519, which nearly every current server accepts.

The keys change twice. Handshake keys, made right after ServerHello, lock the server's certificate messages. Application keys, made from the same secret once the server's Finished is out, lock your data. The Try it unlocks a real handshake with a key log file, so you can see the locked messages by name. Then we'll ask what the router can still learn.

try.title: Unlock your own handshake
steps: In the lab box (a fresh one is fine), make the certificates, point the name `api.pay.test` at 127.0.0.1 (the computer's own address), and start `ApiServer.java`. It's an HTTPS server on port 8443, built on the JDK's own TLS code, and it presents `api-chain.pem`: the leaf and the intermediate.

Capture one request from curl, a command-line program that fetches a web address. `SSLKEYLOGFILE` makes curl write each connection's secrets to a file. That's how tools such as Wireshark and tshark (programs that read captured packets) unlock traffic you own.

sections.h: What the router still sees, and why the hello got bigger
sections.body:
TLS locks the path, the headers and the body of a request, but not everything. A router on the path still sees both addresses, the size and timing of every record, and the whole ClientHello, the server's name included. The DNS lookup for the same name (the question that turned the name into an address, from the lesson before this one) usually crossed the network unlocked too. So the café's Wi-Fi box knows you visited your bank, and about how much you downloaded. "HTTPS hides which site I'm visiting" is wrong for most traffic today.

Encrypted Client Hello (ECH, RFC 9849, March 2026) closes the gap for the name. The server publishes a public key in DNS. The client locks its real ClientHello with that key, and wraps it in an outer ClientHello that names only a shared front door, a server that handles many sites. Both sides must support it, and browsers do. Neither the JDK 25 client nor the lab box's curl sends it, as the Try it shows.

The second change is in the key share. Anyone can record today's handshake and keep it. Suppose someone later builds a large quantum computer, a new kind of machine that could undo X25519 quickly, and the old recording unlocks. People call this "harvest now, decrypt later". So clients now offer a hybrid group, **X25519MLKEM768** (RFC 10024, August 2026, code number 0x11EC). It runs X25519 and ML-KEM-768, a key exchange designed to resist quantum computers, side by side, and mixes both results into one secret. An attacker would have to break both. By April 2026, more than 65% of human traffic to Cloudflare, a company that carries traffic for a large share of the world's websites, used a key exchange like this. Certificates still use the older kind of signature, and that can wait: a recording can't help anyone forge a signature in a handshake that is already over.

The cost is size. JDK 25 offers X25519MLKEM768 first, and that key share alone is 1,216 bytes: 1,184 for ML-KEM and 32 for X25519. The whole ClientHello comes to 1,614 bytes. A packet on most networks carries at most 1,500 bytes (lesson 4 of this track called that limit the MTU), so the hello travels as two TCP segments (TCP's word for its packets). curl, built on the lab box's OpenSSL 3.0 (a free library of encryption code that many programs use), offers only x25519 and sends 517 bytes.

Resumption makes the next connection cheaper. The server's NewSessionTicket, which you saw in the last Try it, is a key the client may show next time to skip the certificate and the signature. With it, the client may even send data in its very first flight. That's **0-RTT** (zero round trips), or early data. The catch is written in RFC 9846: "There are no guarantees of non-replay between connections." Someone who recorded the early data can send it again, and the server may act on it twice. Reading a payment's status twice harms nobody. Approving a payment twice charges the customer twice. **Early data can arrive twice. Send only requests that are safe to repeat.**

Next, we'll turn the check around and make the client prove who it is.

Type 1 is a ClientHello, type 2 a ServerHello. curl offers one share, group 29 (0x001D, x25519) with 32 bytes, and the server takes it. The JDK offers group 4588 (0x11EC, X25519MLKEM768) with 1,216 bytes, plus x25519 as a fallback. The server picks the hybrid group and answers with 1,120 bytes. tshark 4.2 is older than RFC 10024, which is why it prints the number and, with `-V`, "Unknown (0x11ec)". Here the 1,680-byte frame fits in one packet, because `lo` (loopback, the computer talking to itself) allows 65,536 bytes. The lab's capture comes from the lab network, where the same hello is cut into two segments. Neither ClientHello carries an encrypted_client_hello extension, so neither uses ECH. The JDK ended up with HTTP/1.1 because ALPN lets the server choose, and the JDK's HttpsServer speaks only HTTP/1.1.

sections.h: Mutual TLS: the server checks the client's certificate too
sections.body:
A bank that moves money wants proof from the caller, too. An API key, a secret string the caller sends with every request, proves only that the caller knows the string, and a string can leak. The bank wants proof that this is the checkout program of a company it has a contract with. Mutual TLS (**mTLS**) runs the same checks in the other direction. Both sides show a passport.

In TLS 1.3 the server adds a CertificateRequest to its locked first flight. The client answers with its own Certificate and CertificateVerify, signed with its own private key, right before its Finished. The server walks the client's chain exactly as the client walked the server's. Then it maps the certificate to a caller: `CN=checkout,O=Pay Test` may approve payments, and nobody else may. Banks use mTLS for exactly this. A private key that never leaves one computer is harder to leak than a secret that travels in every request.

The order of the messages holds a surprise. The client sends its certificate and its Finished in one flight, and thinks the handshake is done. The server checks the certificate after that. If it rejects it, the client finds out only when it next reads from the connection. So the error shows up on the first request, not in the handshake. The JDK reports `HTTP/1.1 header parser received no bytes`, caused by `Connection reset` (the other side closed the connection abruptly). That looks like a network problem, and it isn't one.

Most TLS failures come down to one of the checks in this lesson. The Try it produces these three:

| What is wrong | curl says | the JDK says |
|---|---|---|
| the host name isn't in the certificate | `no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name` | `No subject alternative DNS name matching localhost found.` |
| the server doesn't send its intermediate | `unable to get local issuer certificate` | `PKIX path building failed`, `unable to find valid certification path to requested target` |
| mTLS, and the client has no certificate | `tlsv13 alert certificate required` | `HTTP/1.1 header parser received no bytes`, root cause `Connection reset` |

A CA that your client doesn't trust produces the same PKIX error as a missing intermediate. (PKIX is the name of the certificate rules in RFC 5280, and the JDK uses it in its messages.) Read the error as "I couldn't build a chain to anything I trust", then find the missing link. `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -showcerts` prints exactly what the server sends.

Every check in this lesson has a price: one more round trip, a bigger hello, a certificate that expires. It's paid once per connection, and the next lesson's protocol decides how many connections a program opens.

try.title: Break the handshake three ways
steps: In the lab box, keep the certificates in `/tmp/pki` and `api.pay.test` in `/etc/hosts` (the file that maps names to addresses on this computer) as before. Start three servers: a correct one on port 8443, one that asks for client certificates (`--mtls`) on 8444, and one that sends only its leaf certificate (`--chain api.pem`) on 8445.
Call each one with curl and with `Handshake.java`. Predict each error before you read it, then match it to the table above.

failed: javax.net.ssl.SSLHandshakeException: (certificate_unknown) PKIX path building failed: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target
  root cause: sun.security.provider.certpath.SunCertPathBuilderException: unable to find valid certification path to requested target
== mTLS, no certificate
curl: (56) OpenSSL SSL_read: OpenSSL/3.0.13: error:0A00045C:SSL routines::tlsv13 alert certificate required, errno 0
failed: java.io.IOException: HTTP/1.1 header parser received no bytes
  root cause: java.net.SocketException: Connection reset
== mTLS, with one
hello from api.pay.test, client CN=checkout,O=Pay Test
200 HTTP_1_1  TLSv1.3 TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384  529 ms

```

In the first case the certificate is fine, but `localhost` isn't one of its names. In the second, the chain stops at the leaf, and both clients say so in their own words. In the third, look at curl's error: it comes from `SSL_read`, reading the answer, and not from the handshake. The client had already finished its side when the server's `certificate required` alert came back. (An alert is TLS's message for "something went wrong".) The JDK, reading the response, found the connection reset. With the client certificate, the server knows exactly who called. The `(certificate_unknown)` in the JDK's messages is the alert the client sends the server before it gives up.

aside.title: Why not switch the check off when it gets in the way?
aside.body: It's tempting, and it's common. Someone hits `PKIX path building failed`, finds a snippet online that trusts every certificate (or uses `curl -k`, or a trust-all setting), and ships it. The connection is still encrypted, but the client now accepts any certificate, including one that an attacker on the path presents. That removes the authentication this lesson is about. Each error means that one check failed, so find which one. A missing intermediate is fixed on the server, a private CA by adding that one root to your trust store, and a wrong name by calling the name on the certificate.

The JDK sends two key shares so that a server without ML-KEM can still take x25519 without a HelloRetryRequest. It pays for that safety with a second TCP segment on every new connection.

steps.say: Take curl's ClientHello from the lab's capture. Each pair of characters below is one byte written in hexadecimal (base 16), so `16` means 22 and `02 00` means 512. The TLS record starts at byte 66 of the captured frame (`0x42`), after 14 bytes of Ethernet header, 20 of IP header (the addresses) and 32 of TCP header. First come 5 bytes of record header, then 4 of handshake header.

lab.title: A ClientHello parser and a certificate chain checker
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 16 fail. `TlsNames.kt` is finished: it holds the names of groups, cipher suites and versions. The tests read four real captures from `src/test/resources/sfz/net/l10/` (curl's and the JDK's ClientHello from the lab network, and the server's answer to each). They also read eleven certificates that `make-certs.sh` in the same folder made with fixed dates.

In `TlsHello.kt`, write `parseClientHello`. Read the record header, and check its length against the bytes you have, so that a hello missing its second segment is rejected. Then read the handshake header and the fixed fields, and walk over the extensions, decoding the five the lab needs. The comment above the function has the byte layout.
Write `parseServerHello` with the same walk over the extensions.

In `ChainCheck.kt`, write `hostMatches`, then `check`. Walk up from the leaf. For each certificate, find its issuer, verify the signature, check that the issuer is a CA, and check the dates. Then match the name. `ChainCheckTest` sets the clock to 10 November 2026. It also asks the JDK's own chain checker (its PKIX validator) about the same chains, so you can see your walk agree with it. Run the tests until all 16 pass.
hints: A `ByteBuffer` keeps the read position for you. Read a length into a variable before you move: `b.position(b.position() + u8(b))` reads the position first and lands one byte short. (The reference solution had exactly this bug until the tests caught it.)
Collect the extensions into a `Map<Int, ByteBuffer>` keyed by type, then decode only the ones you need. curl sends 12 extensions and the JDK sends 13; skip the rest by their length.
The handshake length is 3 bytes: `(u8 shl 16) or u16`. Every other length here is 1 or 2 bytes, and each says how many bytes follow it.

`cert.issuerX500Principal == next.subjectX500Principal` compares names, and names can be copied: `forged.pem` names the real intermediate as its issuer. Only `cert.verify(issuer.publicKey)` proves that the issuer signed it.
`subjectAlternativeNames` returns two-element lists, `[type, value]`, or null. Type 2 is a DNS name.

In `hostMatches`, lower-case both sides. For a pattern `*.pay.test` the host must end with `.pay.test`, and what is left in front must be one label (one part between dots): not empty, and with no dots.

drill.title: Write hostMatches from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `hostMatches(pattern: String, host: String): Boolean` with the rules from the lab: case doesn't matter, and a `*` may only be the whole leftmost part of the name, where it covers exactly one part. Then list, one line each, the four checks a client makes on every certificate of a chain.

recap: A router on the path can read and change plain bytes. TLS locks them with a symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM, using a key that a key exchange agrees on in the open: only public values cross the network.

A certificate ties a name (in its SAN list) to a public key, and a CA signs it. The server sends its leaf and intermediate, and the client walks up to a root in its trust store, checking the signature, the CA flag and the dates at each step, and the name at the leaf.

TLS 1.3 takes one round trip: ClientHello and ServerHello in the open with key shares, then EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished, locked. Add TCP's handshake, and a new connection waits two round trips before the request leaves.
X25519MLKEM768 protects today's recordings against future quantum computers, and makes the JDK 25 ClientHello 1,614 bytes: two packets instead of one.
In mTLS the server checks the client's certificate too. A rejected client certificate shows up on the first read as a reset connection, not as a handshake error.

The limit: TLS leaves the addresses, the record sizes and the server's name in the ClientHello for anyone to see, and ECH hides the name only where both ends support it. 0-RTT early data can be replayed, so it's only for requests that are safe to repeat.
closing:
We started in a café, on its Wi-Fi, trusting a padlock. Now we know what it promises: nobody on the way can read or change the bytes, and a chain of signatures proves who is on the other end. It doesn't hide the site's name, or how much you downloaded.

Next time you see the padlock, click it and open the certificate. Find the list of names (the SAN), the issuer and the two dates, and count how many days the certificate lives.

Next, we'll look inside the locked connection at HTTP itself, and ask why a browser opens six connections to one site when one would seem to do.

quiz.q: Your Kotlin program calls another company's server and fails with `PKIX path building failed: unable to find valid certification path to requested target`. The same address opens fine in Chrome on your laptop. What is the most likely cause?
options: The company's server sends its leaf certificate without the intermediate; Chrome fetched the missing one, and the JDK doesn't
Your program sends the wrong server name (SNI)
quiz.why: `PKIX path building failed` means the JDK couldn't build a chain from the leaf to any root it trusts. Browsers often download a missing intermediate from the address written in the certificate. The JDK doesn't, so a server that forgets to send it works in a browser and fails in your program. An expired certificate fails in Chrome too, with a different message, and JDK 25 speaks TLS 1.3. `openssl s_client -showcerts` shows what the server really sends.

quiz.q: On a resumed TLS 1.3 connection (one that reuses a ticket from an earlier connection), your program could send one request as 0-RTT early data. Which one is safe to send that way?
options: None: early data is sent unlocked
quiz.why: Early data is locked, but RFC 9846 gives no promise that it can't be replayed on another connection. Whoever recorded it can send it again, and the server may act on it twice. Reading a status twice harms nobody. A replayed approval or refund moves money twice. The last option is the opposite mistake: 0-RTT data is encrypted, and what it lacks is protection against replay.

quiz.q: Which handshake message proves that the server holds the private key that belongs to the certificate it sent?
quiz.why: A certificate is public, so sending one proves nothing. CertificateVerify is a signature over the whole handshake so far, made with the private key, and the client checks it with the public key inside the leaf certificate. Finished proves that nobody changed the messages, using keys from the key exchange, but it says nothing about the certificate's key. ServerHello carries only the server's choices and its key share.

quiz.q: A bank's server uses mTLS and rejects your program's client certificate. Your JDK HttpClient doesn't report a handshake error. It logs `IOException: HTTP/1.1 header parser received no bytes`, root cause `Connection reset`. Why?
options: The bank's network drops packets after the handshake
In TLS 1.3 the client sends its certificate with its Finished and moves on; the server checks it afterwards, so the rejection arrives when the client reads the answer
The JDK can't send client certificates over HTTP/1.1
The client certificate's key is too short for TLS 1.3
quiz.why: The client's Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished go out in one flight, and from the client's side the handshake is complete. The server checks the chain after that. On a rejection it sends an alert and closes the connection, which the client meets on its first read. curl shows the same order: its error comes from `SSL_read`, and the alert is `certificate required`. A network problem would not hit only this one server, every time.

quiz.q: Lesson 7 of this track, TCP connections, showed TCP's own handshake. Your program opens a new TCP connection with TLS 1.3 to a bank 70 ms away there and back, and it already knows the bank's address. About how long until the bank receives the first byte of your request?
quiz.why: TCP's first two messages, SYN and SYN-ACK, take one round trip (70 ms), and the ClientHello goes out right after the final ACK. The ClientHello and the server's answer take a second round trip (140 ms). Then the client sends Finished and the request, which need another half round trip to arrive: about 175 ms. 280 ms would be TLS 1.2's two-round-trip handshake plus TCP's. A connection from a pool skips all of it and pays only the 35 ms.

flashcards.front: What is a key share in a TLS 1.3 ClientHello?
flashcards.back: A public value for one group (kind of key exchange) that the client guesses the server will pick, sent before any answer. Guessing is how TLS 1.3 saves a round trip.

flashcards.front: Where does a client look for the server's name in a certificate?
flashcards.back: In the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) list. The old CN field is ignored, and a `*` covers exactly one leftmost part of the name.

flashcards.front: What does the JDK's `PKIX path building failed` mean?
flashcards.back: It couldn't build a chain from the leaf to any root it trusts. Usually the server didn't send its intermediate, or the CA is a private one that isn't in the trust store.

flashcards.front: What can a router on the path see of a TLS 1.3 connection?
flashcards.back: Both addresses and ports, the size and timing of every record, and the whole ClientHello, the server's name included, unless ECH is used.

flashcards.front: Why may 0-RTT early data only carry requests that are safe to repeat?
flashcards.back: Whoever recorded it can replay it on a new connection, so the server may act on it twice.
The hybrid key exchange of RFC 10024 (code 0x11EC): X25519 plus ML-KEM-768, which resists quantum computers. Its client key share is 1,216 bytes.

flashcards.front: In mTLS over TLS 1.3, when does a client learn that its certificate was rejected?
flashcards.back: On its first read after the handshake, because the server checks the client's certificate after the client's Finished.

terms.plain: A way for two sides to work out the same secret from public values, so the key itself never travels.
A signed document saying that a public key belongs to a name, between two dates.
A company that checks who owns a name and signs certificates that clients accept.
The list of root CA certificates a client trusts without proof. JDK 25 has 118.
A CA certificate between the root and the leaf. The server must send it along with its leaf.
The server's name in the ClientHello, sent unlocked so the server can pick the right certificate.
A public value the client sends in advance, for a group it guesses the server will pick.
TLS where the client also shows a certificate and proves it holds the matching private key.

explain_back.prompt: A friend says: "My app talks to the bank over HTTPS, so nobody in between can see anything, and the certificate check is a formality I can switch off while I test." Explain to them what TLS protects, what it leaves visible, and what the certificate check is for.
explain_back.answer: TLS locks everything after the ServerHello: the path, the headers, the body and the answers. Nobody on the way can read them or change them without being caught. It doesn't hide the two addresses, the size and timing of each record, or the ClientHello, which names the server in plain text, and the DNS lookup before it is usually unlocked too. The keys come from a key exchange, and a key exchange on its own would happily run with an attacker sitting between you and the bank. The certificate check stops that. The bank's server proves, with a chain of signatures up to a root you trust and a signature over this very handshake, that it holds the key for its name. Switch the check off and the locking still works, but you no longer know who you're talking to. While testing, I'd add the test CA to the trust store instead, because trust-all code has a habit of reaching the real app.

deeper.body:
**Certificate Transparency.** Public CAs must record every certificate they issue in public logs that can only be added to, and browsers reject certificates that weren't logged. You can search the logs (for example at crt.sh) for every certificate ever issued for a company's names. That's how certificates issued by mistake, or to the wrong person, get noticed.

**Why TLS 1.3 pretends to be TLS 1.2.** The old version number 0x0303, the 32-byte session id and the empty Change Cipher Spec records you saw in the Try it exist for one reason. Early tests of TLS 1.3 failed on old network boxes that dropped anything that didn't look like TLS 1.2. RFC 9846 calls the workaround middlebox compatibility mode. The same thinking explains GREASE: browsers send made-up cipher suite and extension numbers, so that servers that choke on unknown values get noticed and fixed.

**Forcing a HelloRetryRequest.** `openssl s_client -connect api.pay.test:8443 -groups secp384r1:x25519`, against a server that accepts only x25519, shows the extra round trip. The first ClientHello carries a share for secp384r1, the server answers with a HelloRetryRequest naming x25519, and a second ClientHello follows. Your capture then has two Client Hello lines on one connection.

**mTLS inside a company.** Big companies often split one program into many small ones that talk over the network. A tool called a service mesh can give every one of them mTLS without code changes. A helper program runs next to each one, holds a short-lived certificate (often valid for hours, not days) from the company's own CA, and replaces it automatically. What it can't do is decide which calls the business rules allow. It only tells your code which program is calling.
